tldr: For ceiling layouting (precise line drawing) using a drone, researchers developed an end-effector combining a spring-damper-based Gough-Stewart mechanism with actuated omniwheels, achieving millimeter-level drawing precision without requiring detailed modeling or complex control of the aerial vehicle.
hero_caption: Configuration of the proposed end-effector and overview of the ceiling layouting system. (a) Passive Gough-Stewart mechanism using spring-dampers and three actuated omniwheels, (b) drone performing layouting flight while pressing against the ceiling, and (c) upward-facing camera on the lower base tracking a ChArUco board on the underside of the upper platform to estimate relative pose with high precision.
overview:
On construction sites, ceiling layouting—marking positions for piping and drill holes—is a hazardous and strenuous task performed at height. It requires millimeter-level precision to prevent cumulative errors. While aerial robots (drones) offer easy access to high places, contact disturbances and drone oscillations have historically limited aerial manipulation accuracy to the centimeter scale. Previous attempts to achieve high precision have integrated delta-arm mechanisms with drone control, but they rely on precise vehicle identification and complex model predictive control, posing a major barrier to real-world deployment.

To address this, the authors adopted an approach of "letting clever mechanical design shoulder the control burden." Inspired by how humans rest their hands on a desk to write stably, they developed a passive Gough-Stewart mechanism. It provides multiple contact points pressed against the ceiling to stabilize the vehicle, along with mechanical compliance to absorb drone vibrations. Furthermore, they placed actively driven omniwheels on the top platform to rapidly cancel out positioning errors, creating a self-contained smart end-effector.

In real-world flight experiments, ablation studies verified the roles of contact points and active control in boosting precision. Subsequent tests tracing circular trajectories and cursive text ("Hello") showed that the system consistently achieves millimeter-level accuracy (mean error under 3 mm) without any additional tuning of the drone's existing controller.
contributions: Mechanical design of a Gough-Stewart end-effector for ceiling layouting, combining compliant spring-damper support with active actuation via three omniwheels.
A geometric parameter optimization method for the Gough-Stewart mechanism based on Hessian analysis of the potential energy field to maximize restoring stability to the nominal pose.
Implementation of a self-contained tracking system using an upward-facing camera and a ChArUco marker board, enabling sub-millimeter relative pose estimation without occlusion against the ceiling.

Experimental demonstration of millimeter-accurate trajectory tracking on ceilings, matching the precision of state-of-the-art full-body MPC methods without requiring vehicle model identification or retuning of the drone's controller.

sections.heading: Why Millimeter-Level Ceiling Layouting Matters for Drones
sections.summary: Ceiling layouting on construction sites is dangerous work at height requiring millimeter precision, where mistakes cannot be tolerated. However, conventional aerial contact manipulation has been limited to centimeter accuracy, and existing high-precision approaches heavily depend on complex full-body control and exhaustive system identification.
sections.details:
As automation enters the construction industry, marking reference points for piping, ducts, and anchor holes on ceilings ("layouting") remains largely manual. It carries both the risks of working at heights and the strict requirement for installation accuracy. Tolerances for this task are below 5 mm (millimeter accuracy); small cumulative errors can lead to costly rework.

Drones can easily reach elevated areas, but contact-based tasks in flight make them highly vulnerable to disturbances. Aerial robots developed for non-destructive testing focused on maintaining contact force and surface tracking stability, where centimeter-level end-effector positioning was acceptable. Conversely, studies aiming for millimeter precision by mounting parallel mechanisms like delta arms on top of drones faced drawbacks: solving the coupled dynamics between arm and drone required complex full-body control such as nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC), making the system fragile to model uncertainties. In addition, arms alone can only compensate for translational errors; vehicle tilt directly leads to drawing offsets.

To solve this, this work proposes a novel end-effector inspired by how people stabilize their wrists on a desk when writing. By combining "multiple contact points," "compliance," and "active actuation at the tip," it absorbs and compensates for disturbances within the end-effector itself without complicating the drone's control architecture.

sections.heading: Four Design Objectives to Achieve Millimeter Precision
sections.summary: To meet drawing tolerances below 5 mm while keeping the control system simple and robust, the authors leveraged mechanical intelligence. They established four design objectives: compliance, multiple contact points, actuation, and self-containment.
sections.details:
For practical use on construction sites, requiring complex vehicle modeling or per-environment control retuning is a major hurdle. Rather than relying on complicated control, the authors aimed to achieve high precision through mechanical intelligence. They formulated four core design objectives:

- Compliance: Springs and dampers between the marking tip and the aerial vehicle isolate the contact point from in-flight oscillations and disturbances.
- Multiple contact points: Instead of pressing a single tool tip, engaging multiple contact points against the ceiling leverages contact constraints to strongly stabilize vehicle roll and pitch.
- Actuation: Actuators on the tip drive the mechanism smoothly across the ceiling while actively and instantaneously counteracting position tracking errors of the drone.
- Self-containment: The end-effector operates as an independent add-on module regardless of the specific drone platform or its autopilot, eliminating the need to retune vehicle parameters.

sections.heading: Blending a Passive Stewart Mechanism with Active Omniwheels
sections.summary: Geometrically optimizing a Gough-Stewart mechanism supported by six spring-dampers created a stable structure that autonomously centers itself. The upper platform carries three actuated omniwheels and an onboard vision tracker, creating a loosely coupled control architecture with the drone.
sections.details:
The proposed end-effector is built upon a 6-DOF Gough-Stewart parallel mechanism.

### III-A & III-B: Passive Gough-Stewart Mechanism and Stability Analysis
Six commercial shock absorbers (using water damping) are arranged and tuned so that a 15 N upward push against the ceiling compresses the legs to the stroke center ($h_{nom}$, mid-point of the 2–4 cm travel range). Because the legs are passive, restoring stability—the ability of the upper platform to return to center after a perturbation—is critical. A naive geometry (equal base and platform radii) suffers from bistability, where the platform can tip outward and get trapped at workspace boundaries. The authors formulated an optimization problem to maximize the minimum eigenvalue $\lambda_{min}$ of the Hessian of the potential energy field under displacement. A larger minimum eigenvalue ensures stronger restoring forces toward the center across all directions. The optimization yielded a stable geometry with a clear global energy minimum at the nominal center.

### III-C & III-D: End-Effector Control and Tracking
The upper platform features three custom 100 mm carbon-fiber omniwheels, each driven by a servomotor. A cascaded controller—an inner PI velocity loop and an outer P position loop with velocity feedforward—regulates 3-DOF planar motion ($x, y, \theta$). Because the top platform is sandwiched between the ceiling and drone and hidden from external motion capture, an upward-facing camera with a ring light on the lower base tracks a ChArUco marker board under the top platform, delivering relative pose estimation with sub-millimeter precision.

### III-E: Drone Interface
The drone and end-effector are decoupled in control. Both receive the same global planar reference trajectory ($x, y, \text{yaw}$). However, the drone's Z position is simply commanded to a constant height that compresses the end-effector to its nominal stroke, requiring no complex coordinated communication between the two systems.

captions.F3: Comparison of potential energy fields at equilibrium height between the optimized geometry (top) and a naive geometry (bottom). The optimized design exhibits a distinct global minimum at the center ($X=0, Y=0$), demonstrating high stability that naturally restores the platform after disturbances.

sections.heading: Hardware Experiments: Ablation and Drawing Precision
sections.summary: Ablation tests confirmed the crucial roles of multiple contact points and active feedback control. In continuous circular and cursive text drawing experiments, the end-effector consistently maintained millimeter-level precision even when drone tracking drifted by several centimeters.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted by mounting the end-effector on an omnidirectional hexacopter (OMAV) with tiltable arms, marking against an MDF board fixed to the ceiling. The vehicle's controller used baseline parameters without payload tuning.

### IV-A: Tracking Accuracy Verification
Static validation using an external Vicon motion capture system verified that the onboard camera tracker achieves a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.8 mm in the XY plane and 0.2 degrees in yaw, confirming sufficient measurement fidelity.

### IV-C: Ablation Study
The effect of each design component was evaluated on a 250 mm radius circular trajectory:
- Free flight baseline: Drone tracking error alone was coarse, with an MAE of 22.6 mm (90th percentile at 43.5 mm).
- Single contact point (rigid): Stick-slip friction against the ceiling aggravated oscillations, performing worse than free flight.
- Passive 3-point contact (bearings): Rigidly supported 3-point contact alone cut the drone's MAE in half via contact constraints.
- Compliant + Actuated (with FB): Yielded the most dramatic improvement, dropping the end-effector MAE to below 1.5 mm—an order of magnitude better. Active omniwheels maintained low friction along the travel path while actively eliminating lateral slip.

### IV-D & IV-E: Trajectory Tracking, Repeatability, and Speed Sweep
In 10 consecutive laps around a 250 mm circle, the end-effector maintained an MAE below 2 mm, even when vehicle tracking error spiked up to 35 mm. Circles with radii from 50 mm to 250 mm exhibited similar accuracy.
Furthermore, cursive "Hello" text was drawn under five velocity and acceleration levels (up to 27.5 cm/s and 13.75 cm/s²). While prior work (Tzoumanikas et al. using full-body NMPC with a delta arm) reported errors between 2.1 and 2.8 mm, the proposed system achieved an MAE of 1.74 mm at low speeds and stayed below 3 mm (with worst-case error MWCE under 4 mm) at maximum speed, matching or exceeding state-of-the-art accuracy without complex full-body control.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: This study showed that combining compliant kinematics with active actuation enables millimeter precision in ceiling contact tasks using a straightforward control structure. Future work will investigate non-horizontal/curved surfaces and integrated full-body control.
sections.details:
This paper presented and validated a novel aerial end-effector for high-precision ceiling layouting on construction sites.

By leveraging "smart mechanics"—physical stabilization via multiple contact points, disturbance isolation through spring-dampers, and active position error rejection via tip omniwheels—the system reliably achieves practical millimeter accuracy (<5 mm tolerance, measured at 1–3 mm) without complex system identification or advanced full-body drone controllers.

Future research directions include adapting the mechanism to inclined ceilings and curved surfaces, accommodating alternative inspection tools or drone platforms, and exploring whether combining this mechanism with full-body integrated control can yield further performance gains.

takeaways: A prime example of "solving challenges mechanically before overcomplicating control": combining multiple ceiling contact points with passive spring-dampers provides exceptional attitude stabilization during aerial contact.

When designing passive parallel linkages, eigenvalue analysis of the potential energy Hessian mathematically guides geometric parameter selection to ensure self-restoring behavior across the entire workspace.
Even with base vehicle tracking errors spanning several centimeters, localized high-bandwidth translational feedback at the tool tip can elevate overall task precision to the millimeter scale.
For job-site deployment, a modular "self-contained end-effector" that treats the carrier drone as a black box substantially enhances practical adoption.
limitations: The current mechanism is designed solely for horizontal, flat ceiling surfaces and cannot handle steps, slopes, or curved walls/ceilings.

If the drone experiences rapid position jumps or strong wind gusts exceeding the end-effector's stroke allowance (around 2–4 cm), the mechanism reaches physical limits and millimeter precision breaks down.
Vertical force/compression control is operated open-loop at a fixed nominal height, with no active altitude adjustment mechanism to handle ceiling waviness or construction tolerances.
